brief.outcome: Get the share of open invoices that are past due under 15% within three months, without losing any retainer clients.

answers.question: Business and billing?
answers.answer: Marketing agency with 55 retainer clients, invoiced monthly on 30-day terms in FreshBooks.

answers.question: How bad is it?
answers.answer: About 40% of open invoices are past due (FreshBooks aging report, reported), worst ones over 90 days.

answers.question: What happens now?
answers.answer: Reminders are sent by hand when someone remembers.

answers.question: What access and rules?
answers.answer: FreshBooks MCP with draft access; emails to clients go out only after I approve them.

answers.question: Target and constraint?
answers.answer: Overdue share under 15% within three months without losing clients.

answers.question: Data home and decider?
answers.answer: Keep data in this project. I decide.

research.approach: Practitioners clean the receivables first, so nobody is chased for a paid or disputed invoice, then age and rank what is left. They separate clients who are late from clients who are unhappy, because reminders do not fix disputes. A dated cadence runs from a courtesy reminder before the due date through a friendly nudge, a firmer follow-up with a phone call, and a formal notice with a deadline. The worst accounts get a call and a short written payment plan, and new work is paused on seriously overdue accounts. Prevention comes from clear written terms, the right billing contact and a card or direct debit on file for retainers. Every contact is logged and the overdue share is tracked weekly.

steps.name: Clean the receivables before chasing
steps.why: Reconcile payments so only truly outstanding invoices are chased; unapplied payments, credits and disputes must not get reminders.

steps.name: Age, segment and rank what is overdue
steps.why: Ageing buckets by size and client show where the money is and which accounts need a call and which need only a nudge.

steps.name: Find the real reason: late versus unhappy
steps.why: Reminders do not fix a dispute; a call finds out whether the client is late, stuck in approvals, short of cash or unhappy.

steps.name: Prevent lateness: clear terms, right contact, card or direct debit
steps.why: Written terms, the right accounts contact and automatic payment for retainers stop lateness before it starts.

steps.name: Run a dated reminder cadence with an approved tone
steps.why: A pre-due reminder and dated follow-ups catch invoices stuck in approval queues and make chasing routine and polite.

steps.name: Offer short written payment plans and pause work on severe cases
steps.why: Plans of a few instalments with a clear missed-payment consequence recover cash, and pausing new work protects the agency.

steps.name: Log every contact and track the overdue share weekly
steps.why: A written log and a weekly read on one definition show whether the routine works and support any later escalation.

pitfalls.text: Chasing disputed invoices or unpaid ones that have an unapplied payment, which damages the relationship.
Adding late fees that were not disclosed before the work began, or above legal limits.
Letting invoices pass 90 days with no owner or next step; recovery odds fall sharply.
Lifting a pause or credit hold as soon as a client complains, or extending new credit to an account on a payment plan.
Looking only at average days outstanding and missing a few severely late accounts.
Not logging contacts, and charging a saved card without the client's agreement.

hypotheses.statement: Invoices go late mainly because reminders are sent by hand and irregularly.
hypotheses.test: Compare days late for clients who were reminded with those who were not, using the owner's list of past reminders.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Reminded invoices are paid sooner than similar unreminded ones.
hypotheses.refute_if: Reminded and unreminded invoices are paid at the same speed.

hypotheses.statement: A handful of clients hold most of the overdue money, so the fix is account by account.
hypotheses.test: Share of overdue value by client, and how many clients are late on most invoices.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A small number of clients hold most of the overdue value.
hypotheses.refute_if: Lateness is spread across many clients.

hypotheses.statement: Some of the oldest invoices are held back by a dispute or unhappiness with the work, not slow payment.
hypotheses.test: Call or review notes for clients over 90 days and mark each as late, stuck or disputing.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Several of the over-90-day invoices have a stated dispute.

hypotheses.statement: Invoices go to the wrong person or get stuck in client approvals.
hypotheses.test: Compare the billing contact on file with the accounts contact and check bounce or no-open signs.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Late clients have no accounts contact on file or a changed one.
hypotheses.refute_if: Contacts are right and invoices are seen.

hypotheses.statement: Retainer clients with a card or direct debit on file pay on time and the rest do not.
hypotheses.test: Compare days late by payment method.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Automatic payers are clearly later less often than invoice payers.

hypotheses.statement: The 40% figure overstates or understates the problem because it mixes count and value or includes paid invoices.
hypotheses.test: Recompute from the invoice list after matching payments, by count and by value.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The checked share differs from 40% on either basis.
hypotheses.refute_if: The checked share is about 40% on both.

measurement.window: Weekly for three months from the first approved reminder; the target is judged at the end of the third month.
measurement.min_volume: At least eight weekly readings on the same definition before any claim, as 55 clients make weekly swings large.
measurement.stop_rule: Stop chasing a client and tell the owner the same day if the client disputes the invoice, threatens to leave, or a promise is broken twice; stop all steps if a client is lost because of them.
